content.title: Solving Exponential Equations with a Common Base
content.overview: This lesson focuses on solving exponential equations by rewriting both sides of the equation as powers of the same base. Once the bases are identical, the exponents can be set equal to solve for the unknown variable.
learning_objectives: Identify equations where both sides can be expressed using a common base.
Apply exponent rules to rewrite terms and combine exponents into a single power on each side.
Solve for the variable by equating exponents and performing a final verification.

sections.title: The Same-Base Strategy
sections.content:
The core principle for solving these equations is the One-to-One Property of Exponents: if b^A = b^B (where b > 0 and b ≠ 1), then A = B. To use this, you must first identify a common base 'b' that can represent every term in the equation. For example, if you see 4 and 8, you should recognize them both as powers of 2 (2^2 and 2^3).

![A flowchart showing the steps: Identify Common Base, Rewrite Terms, Combine Exponents, Equate Exponents, and Solve.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/978c8ce9-e4fb-48df-b825-df1affc131ae-1786505746844-50.webp)

sections.title: Rewriting and Combining Terms
sections.content: Once a common base is identified, rewrite every factor. Use the Product Rule (b^m * b^n = b^{m+n}) and the Power of a Power Rule ((b^m)^n = b^{mn}) to simplify each side into a single base raised to a single expression. Remember that radicals can be written as fractional exponents (e.g., √b = b^(1/2)) and reciprocals as negative exponents (e.g., 1/b = b^-1).

sections.title: Equating and Solving
sections.content: After simplifying the equation to the form b^f(x) = b^g(x), drop the bases and set the exponents equal: f(x) = g(x). This typically results in a linear equation that can be solved using standard algebraic steps. Always substitute your final answer back into the original equation to ensure both sides are numerically equal.

worked_examples.question: Solve for x: 3^(2x - 1) = 9 * √3
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the common base. Both 9 and √3 are powers of 3. Step 2: Rewrite the right side. 9 = 3^2 and √3 = 3^(1/2). So, 9 * √3 = 3^2 * 3^(1/2). Step 3: Combine exponents using the Product Rule. 3^(2 + 1/2) = 3^(5/2). Step 4: Set the exponents equal. The equation is now 3^(2x - 1) = 3^(5/2), so 2x - 1 = 5/2. Step 5: Solve for x. Add 1 to both sides: 2x = 7/2. Divide by 2: x = 7/4.

worked_examples.question: Solve for y: 4^(y+1) = 1/8
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the common base. Both 4 and 8 are powers of 2. Step 2: Rewrite both sides. 4^(y+1) becomes (2^2)^(y+1) = 2^(2y+2). 1/8 becomes 1/(2^3) = 2^-3. Step 3: Set exponents equal. 2y + 2 = -3. Step 4: Solve for y. 2y = -5, so y = -5/2.

common_mistakes: Forgetting to distribute the exponent when using the Power of a Power Rule (e.g., writing (2^2)^(x+1) as 2^(2x+1) instead of 2^(2x+2)).
Treating square roots as whole numbers instead of fractional exponents (e.g., treating √3 as 3 instead of 3^0.5).
Mistaking the base (e.g., trying to use 4 as a base for 8, even though 8 is not an integer power of 4).
exam_tips: Look for 'hidden' bases: 1 can be written as any base to the power of 0 (b^0 = 1).
Memorize common powers of 2, 3, and 5 to quickly identify common bases.
If you are stuck, you can plug the answer choices back into the original equation using a calculator to see which one works.
content.recap: To solve exponential equations with a common base, rewrite both sides as powers of that base, simplify using exponent rules until you have one power on each side, set the exponents equal, and solve for the variable.

knowledge_claims.content: If b^A = b^B and b is a positive number other than 1, then A must equal B.
The first step in the Same-Base Exponent Match strategy is identifying a single positive base that all terms in the equation can be expressed as.
A square root √b is expressed as an exponent of 1/2, such as b^(1/2).
A reciprocal 1/b^n is expressed as a negative exponent, b^-n.
When raising a power to another power, such as (b^m)^n, the exponents must be multiplied: b^(m*n).
When multiplying two terms with the same base, such as b^m * b^n, the exponents must be added: b^(m+n).
A common error is failing to distribute the new base's exponent to all terms in the existing exponent expression.
The number 1 can be rewritten as any base b raised to the power of 0.
After setting exponents equal, the resulting equation is typically a linear equation that must be solved for the variable.
Verification of the solution is performed by substituting the calculated value back into the original equation to ensure both sides match numerically.
If an equation contains 4 and 8, the most effective common base to use is 2, because 4 = 2^2 and 8 = 2^3.
To solve 3^(2x-1) = 3^(5/2), the correct algebraic step is to drop the bases and solve 2x - 1 = 5/2.
